Producing More, Losing More: A Data-Driven Look at Global Agricultural Risk

Global food challenges are often framed as a production problem: grow more, and the problem is solved. But producing more does not necessarily mean that food becomes more available, less wasted, or less exposed to trade risk.

This project explores whether agricultural risk is simply a production problem, or whether inefficiencies, post-harvest losses, and trade exposure across the system also play a role. Using data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) from 2015 to 2024, the analysis examines agricultural productivity, production value, loss, and trade dependency across selected countries and commodities, with trends extending to 2025–2029.

Key question

Is global agricultural risk driven mainly by a deficit in production volumes, or by structural inefficiencies in how food is protected, managed, and traded?

6countries analysed
4commodities tracked
10years of data, 5-year outlook
R² 0.99Random Forest model fit
Scope

Each country represents a different position in the global food system, from productivity benchmark to structurally vulnerable importer, so the comparison covers more than a single story.

Four commodities, spanning staples and livestock

Statistical validation

SPSS validation, then a Random Forest forecast

Production and loss distributions were strongly skewed; yield was comparatively stable. A Random Forest model was then trained on a balanced panel of roughly 200 observations to generate the 2025–2029 forecast.

What the data shows

Growing more food isn't the same as feeding more people

  • 01

    Productivity is wildly unequal. The USA's yields run 3 to 6× higher than Nigeria's across staple crops, and over 40× higher for dairy, a gap driven by land access, infrastructure, and efficiency, not effort.

  • 02

    Post-harvest losses often outpace production gains. In the USA's maize sector, average annual losses run more than 3× higher than the average annual production growth they're meant to offset. Brazil's maize sector shows the same pattern.

  • 03

    Trade is concentrated and fragile. Across the four commodities studied, the top two exporting countries account for 75 to 94% of exports, exposing the wider system to shocks in just a few places.

  • 04

    Per-capita availability has barely moved. Despite real production growth in most countries, food available per person crept up only slightly over the decade, a sign that production gains aren't reliably translating into more food reaching people.

Agricultural risk isn't driven by a shortage of production, most countries in this analysis are producing more, not less. It's driven by structural inefficiencies: unequal productivity, losses that often outpace the production gains they're meant to protect, and exports concentrated in one or two countries per commodity. Strengthening food systems means investing in how they work, not just growing more food.

Limitations

Where to read this carefully

  • Covers 6 countries and 4 commodities, a slice of the global system, not the whole picture.
  • The Random Forest's near-perfect R² (≈0.99) likely reflects some overfitting.
  • FAOSTAT reporting standards vary slightly across countries.
  • Forecasts assume no major structural shocks, climate, policy, or conflict.
